consensus_summary: The blind consensus converges on two tracks: (1) in discipleship and election texts, 'hate' is a Semitic comparative idiom meaning to love less, to subordinate, or to reject/not choose in favor of a supreme loyalty (Luke 14:26; Gen 29:30-31; Mal 1:2-3/Rom 9:13); (2) in ethical texts, hate is literal sinful enmity, the antithesis of love (1 John). Additional common senses include righteous abhorrence of evil and the world's hostility to Christ. Responses A and B make the comparative-preference/rejection idiom primary; C and D make the ethical anti-love sense primary while listing the idiom as a common alternative.
book_summary: The book defines hate as 'to un-choose' — to repudiate a covenant partner or claim in favor of another — enacted through refusal, disfavor, or sending away rather than through feelings of hostility. It explicitly rejects the common softening of the famous texts to 'love less,' insisting hate is an enacted covenantal repudiation, with Love as its opposite.
consensus_core_identification: Hate in Scripture is context-dependent: primarily either (a) a comparative idiom of preference/rejection ('love less,' renounce, covenantal non-election) in discipleship and election texts, or (b) sinful emotional enmity opposed to love in ethical texts.
book_core_identification: Hate is a covenantal act of un-choosing — repudiating a partner or claim in favor of another — enacted by refusal, disfavor, or sending away; it is not an emotion and not merely 'loving less.'
boundary_disagreement: The book keeps the consensus's central referent (hate as rejection/repudiation rather than raw emotion, seen in Responses A and B's 'decisive rejection,' 'renounce its claim,' 'covenantally reject and not choose') but excludes two consensus glosses: (1) the 'love less' comparative softening, which the book explicitly names and rejects in its common-view note, and (2) the plain-emotion sense (hostility, enmity) that Responses C and D treat as primary. Cases like Gen 29:31 and Luke 14:26, which the consensus reads as 'loved less than,' are reclassified as enacted un-choosing/repudiation. The book also foregrounds enacted covenantal disfavor (Hos 9:15's 'drive them out of mine house') as the defining mechanism.
rationale: The book's core — repudiation of a covenant partner or claim in favor of another — sits recognizably inside the consensus's rejection/non-election strand, which Responses A and B state explicitly ('repudiate allegiance,' 'covenantally reject and not choose'). It does not replace the referent; it sharpens it by insisting hate is an enacted un-choosing rather than either an emotion or a diminished degree of love. That insistence is a real boundary disagreement: the consensus's dominant harmonization of Luke 14:26 via Matt 10:37 ('love less') is expressly denied, and the ethical-emotion sense central to Responses C and D is demoted to a mischaracterization. This is a material change of boundary and conditions within the same general category, i.e., REFINED, not DIVERGENT, because 'un-choose/repudiate' and 'reject in favor of another' are substantially the same identification at the center.
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH, since Responses A and B already include 'renounce,' 'repudiate,' and 'covenantally reject and not choose' in their primary meanings, making the book's 'un-choose' just a crisper wording of the existing consensus idiom rather than a material refinement. Against this, the book's explicit repudiation of the 'love less' gloss — which is the consensus's standard harmonization of Luke 14:26 and Gen 29 — and its exclusion of the emotional-enmity sense (primary in C and D) constitute genuine boundary disagreement, not mere phrasing. On citations: Prov 1:29 ('hated knowledge, and did not choose') and Hos 9:15 (hatred enacted as driving out and loving no more) strongly support 'un-choose,' but Gen 29:30-31 explicitly pairs 'hated' with 'loved more than,' which supports the very 'love less' reading the book rejects, and Luke 14:26 alone does not adjudicate between renunciation and comparative love — hence only partial support.
